analysis.one_liner: Orders federal refunds of at least $8.9 billion for California electricity overcharges.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: Senator Boxer introduced it with no cosponsors, and it sat on the Senate calendar until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During California's 2000-2001 electricity crisis, wholesale power sellers charged prices a federal review found excessive. This bill would have amended the Federal Power Act to require the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to order refunds, with interest, of at least $8.9 billion for overcharges between June 2000 and June 2001, and to force renegotiation of the expensive long-term contracts California signed with power companies in early 2001. It was introduced in July 2004 and never reached a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: California electricity ratepayers, who absorbed the costs of the 2000-2001 power crisis, would receive refunds with interest, and the state would have gained relief from high-priced long-term power contracts it signed at the height of the crisis.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to order refunds, plus interest, for charges it finds unjust or unreasonable on electricity sold or transmitted between June 1, 2000, and June 19, 2001, totaling no less than $8.9 billion.

Directs the Commission to order renegotiation of the long-term electricity contracts the State of California signed with energy companies between January 1 and May 31, 2001, when prices were at their peak.
Sets tight deadlines: the refund order within 60 days of enactment and the contract-renegotiation order within 30 days, so the money could not be tied up in indefinite commission proceedings.

analysis.who_pays: The wholesale electricity sellers and energy companies that collected the charges during the crisis would repay the overcharges with interest, and counterparties to California's long-term contracts would face renegotiated, presumably lower, terms.

drawbacks.text: The bill overrides the normal case-by-case process by legislating a minimum refund of $8.9 billion in advance, which critics would call an unconstitutional or at least unfair taking of company revenues without individual findings for each seller.

Forcing renegotiation of signed long-term contracts after the fact would unsettle the wholesale power market's reliance on contracts, a cost borne by anyone who trades or sells electricity under long-term deals.
The refund applies only to California-related charges from a single 13-month window, so customers elsewhere hit by the same period's price spikes get nothing from this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For California ratepayers the upside is large and concrete: up to $8.9 billion in refunds with interest and relief from crisis-era contracts. The main costs fall on the energy companies that collected the charges, with a secondary cost to market confidence in long-term contracts. The bill's weakness is procedural: it predetermines the refund amount rather than letting the commission calculate each seller's overcharge, which would have invited court challenges even if it had passed.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, placed on the Senate calendar, and then simply sat there until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 — no cosponsors joined, no committee acted, and no vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Senator Barbara Boxer introduced the bill in the Senate on July 8, 2004, and it was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 625.
No senator cosponsored the bill, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The bill would have required the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to order refunds of at least $8.9 billion, with interest, for unjust and unreasonable electricity charges from June 2000 through June 2001, and to order renegotiation of California's crisis-era long-term contracts.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The energy companies that sold power into California during the 2000-2001 crisis are better off: because the bill never advanced, no refund order was forced and the crisis-era long-term contracts stand as signed. California ratepayers never received the refunds the bill targeted.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Electricity Gouging Refund Act of 2003 to force refunds of California electricity overcharges, and saw it placed on the Senate calendar.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; after its second reading it sat on the Senate calendar with no scheduling and no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party, and died without a roll call, so no vote breakdown exists — but the one party-line fact on the record is that only a Democrat backed it.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity sellers and energy traders
industries.note: These companies collected the charges during the 2000-2001 California crisis; the bill would have clawed back at least $8.9 billion with interest. Blocking the bill preserved those revenues at the expense of the customers who paid them.
Companies holding California's 2001 long-term contracts would have had to renegotiate them under the bill. Those contracts, signed at crisis prices, remained in force because the bill never advanced.
Not an industry in the usual sense, but the bill's target beneficiaries were California electricity customers, who paid crisis-era prices and would have received the refunds and contract relief.
